The full checkerboard effective Hamiltonian is obtained by summing this local contribution over all nearest-neighbour pairs of crossed plaquettes. Since, the crossed-plaquette centers form a square lattice, each crossed plaquette has coordination number zcb=4z_{\text{cb}}=4. Therefore,

∑⟨α,β⟩(ταz+τβz)=zcb​∑αταz.\sum_{\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle}\left(\tau^{z}_{\alpha}+\tau^{z}_{\beta}\right)=z_{\text{cb}}\sum_{\alpha}\tau^{z}_{\alpha}.

With this convention, the full checkerboard Hamiltonian is

Hcbeff=881∑⟨α,β⟩[3(J(2)−J(1))τxατxβ+(J(1)+J(2)−4J(3)+2J(4))τzατzβ]+3281(J(1)+J(2)−J(3)−J(4))∑ατzα+const.H^{\text{cb}}_{\text{eff}}=\frac{8}{81}\sum_{\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle}\left[3\left(J^{(2)}-J^{(1)}\right)\tau^{x}_{\alpha}\tau^{x}_{\beta}\right.\\ \left.+\left(J^{(1)}+J^{(2)}-4J^{(3)}+2J^{(4)}\right)\tau^{z}_{\alpha}\tau^{z}_{\beta}\right]\\ +\frac{32}{81}\left(J^{(1)}+J^{(2)}-J^{(3)}-J^{(4)}\right)\sum_{\alpha}\tau^{z}_{\alpha}+{\rm const.} (71)

Equation (71) acts on pseudospins τα\tau_{\alpha} residing on the square lattice formed by the centers of the crossed plaquettes. It contains an Ising-like ταx​τβx\tau^{x}_{\alpha}\tau^{x}_{\beta} term, a second Ising-like ταz​τβz\tau^{z}_{\alpha}\tau^{z}_{\beta} term, and a field along the τz\tau^{z} direction. Thus the next-nearest-neighbour perturbation on the checkerboard lattice produces an anisotropic two-component pseudospin model rather than a simple resonance term. In general this is only a correction to the leading local field already generated by the nearest-neighbour perturbation in Eq. (67), so we do not attempt to map out its full phase diagram here.

The situation is much more constrained, and more revealing, on the pyrochlore lattice. There the nearest-neighbour perturbation produces no local pseudospin field, and tetrahedral symmetry further reduces the independent next-nearest-neighbour couplings by imposing J(1)=J(3)J^{(1)}=J^{(3)} and J(2)=J(4)J^{(2)}=J^{(4)}. For the pair of tetrahedra shown in Fig. 5, the two allowed coupling classes are

J(1)\displaystyle J^{(1)} =J16=J36=J25=J27=J17=J35,\displaystyle=J_{16}=J_{36}=J_{25}=J_{27}=J_{17}=J_{35}\,, (72a)
J(2)\displaystyle J^{(2)} =J15=J26=J37.\displaystyle=J_{15}=J_{26}=J_{37}\,. (72b)

Substituting these symmetry constraints into the two-pseudospin Hamiltonian produces a substantial simplification. Three things happen simultaneously. First, the one-body pseudospin field cancels. Second, the anisotropy between the ταx​τβx\tau^{x}_{\alpha}\tau^{x}_{\beta} and ταz​τβz\tau^{z}_{\alpha}\tau^{z}_{\beta} channels disappears. Third, all orientation-dependent information collapses into the two coupling classes J(1)J^{(1)} and J(2)J^{(2)}. Thus, a rather complicated set of projected two-spin matrix elements collapses, by tetrahedral symmetry, to a single U(1)-symmetric nearest-neighbour pseudospin interaction on the diamond lattice:

Heff=827​(J(2)−J(1))​∑⟨α,β⟩(ταx​τβx+ταz​τβz)+const.H_{\text{eff}}=\frac{8}{27}\left(J^{(2)}-J^{(1)}\right)\sum_{\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle}\left(\tau_{\alpha}^{x}\tau_{\beta}^{x}+\tau_{\alpha}^{z}\tau_{\beta}^{z}\right)+\text{const}. (73)

The simplification in Eq. (73) is a key consequence of the pyrochlore symmetry. In contrast with the checkerboard case, a local pseudospin field is not generated on the pyrochlore lattice by the next-nearest-neighour Heisenberg perturbations, just as it was not generated by the nearest-neigbour terms, see Section IV.1. The leading degeneracy-lifting term is instead an interaction between neighbouring tetrahedra. Thus the two-dimensional singlet space on each tetrahedron acts as an effective spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} degree of freedom living on the diamond lattice of tetrahedron centers. The leading symmetry-allowed next-nearest-neighbour Heisenberg perturbation does not merely select a static valence-bond orientation; it generates a genuine collective pseudospin dynamics. Moreover, the dynamics has an emergent continuous symmetry: the Hamiltonian is invariant under rotations in the τx\tau^{x}–τz\tau^{z} plane, generated by τy\tau^{y}. Equivalently, after a relabelling of pseudospin axes, it is the standard quantum spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} XY model on the diamond lattice. The coupling may be ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic depending on the sign of J(2)−J(1)J^{(2)}-J^{(1)}.

The absence of an effective Zeeman field on the pyrochlore lattice is as important as the form of the interaction itself. It means that no particular local valence-bond orientation is selected by the perturbations considered in this and the previous sections. This is a natural consequence of the fact that these perturbations do not break any pyrochlore lattice symmetries and hence cannot result in an effective Hamiltonian that does. Instead, the next-nearest-neighbour Heizenberg perturbation promotes coherent mixing of the two local singlet states on neighbouring tetrahedra. This is the key difference from the checkerboard case.

IV.2.1 Effective interactions for different orientations

The derivation above used the symmetries of the checkerboard and pyrochlore lattices to restrict the number of independent microscopic couplings. Before interpreting Eqs. (71) and (73), we must check one further point. The local pseudospin basis |A⟩,|B⟩|A\rangle,|B\rangle is a convenient basis, but it is not invariant under rotations of a crossed plaquette or tetrahedron. A spatial rotation acts nontrivially inside the two-dimensional local valence-bond space. Thus, even if the microscopic Heisenberg interaction is fully symmetric, its projection could in principle generate bond-dependent directional pseudospin couplings. In other words, the projection might have produced a compass-like or spin-orbit-like effective Hamiltonian rather than the simple form obtained above, as seen in related pyrochlore quantum dimer models [7].

It is therefore nontrivial that the present construction does not lead to an orientation-dependent pseudospin Hamiltonian at this order. We show this explicitly below. In deriving Eqs. (71) and (73), we considered the pairs shown in Figs. 4 and 5. Other pairs are obtained by a C4C_{4} rotation for the checkerboard lattice and a C3C_{3} rotation for the pyrochlore lattice. Since the local pseudospin basis itself rotates nontrivially, the matrix elements must be checked rather than assumed to be identical.

Figure 6 shows the same pair of singlet configurations on two adjacent tetrahedra in two different orientations. The numbering of the sites in the two panels is related by a 2​π/32\pi/3 rotation about the axis perpendicular to the page and passing through site 22. The leading two-spin matrix elements are calculated by the same loop-resolution procedure as before [see Appendix C]. The results are listed in Table 2.

Comparing Table 2 with Table 1, we see that the entries are cycled in a definite way. Sites 1,2,31,2,3 are replaced by 2,3,12,3,1, while sites 5,6,75,6,7 are replaced by 6,7,56,7,5, respectively. For example, ⟨ee¯¯,ee¯¯​|𝐒3⋅𝐒5|​—m—,ee¯¯⟩\langle\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\mathbf{S}_{3}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{5}|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle in the rotated orientation of Fig. 6(b), which is the complex conjugate of ⟨—m—,ee¯¯​|𝐒3⋅𝐒5|​ee¯¯,ee¯¯⟩\langle\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\mathbf{S}_{3}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{5}|\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle, is equal to ⟨ee¯¯,ee¯¯​|𝐒2⋅𝐒7|​—m—,ee¯¯⟩\langle\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\mathbf{S}_{2}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{7}|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle in the original orientation of Fig. 6(a).

Thus, changing from orientation 1 to orientation 2 permutes the two-spin interaction matrices (93)–(109), but only within the respective J(1)J^{(1)} and J(2)J^{(2)} sectors of Eq. (72). After the matrices in each sector are summed, the effective Hamiltonian in Eq. (73) is unchanged. The same conclusion holds for the other two orientations of a neighbouring tetrahedron pair.

On the checkerboard lattice, a C4C_{4} rotation cycles the sites as 1→3→11\rightarrow 3\rightarrow 1 and 5→7→55\rightarrow 7\rightarrow 5, while sites 22 and 66 remain fixed. This again only permutes the interaction matrices within the coupling sectors J(1),J(2),J(3)J^{(1)},J^{(2)},J^{(3)}, and J(4)J^{(4)} defined in Eq. (68). Hence, after all matrices within each sector are added, the checkerboard effective Hamiltonian in Eq. (71) is also independent of the orientation of the plaquette pair.

This orientation independence is a useful structural result. Although the local pseudospin basis transforms nontrivially under rotations, the projected Heisenberg perturbation does not generate bond-dependent compass or spin-orbit couplings at this order. The pyrochlore projection therefore gives the simple diamond-lattice XY model in Eq. (73), rather than a more general bond-dependent pseudospin model.

IV.2.2 Emergent pseudospin dynamics on pyrochlore

Equation (73) is an XY model even though it involves xx and zz pseudospin components rather than the more conventional xx and yy. This is only a rotation of axes in the emergent two-dimensional singlet space on each tetrahedron. Upon defining

σx=τx,σy=τz,σz=−τy,\sigma^{x}=\tau^{x},\qquad\sigma^{y}=\tau^{z},\qquad\sigma^{z}=-\tau^{y},

Eq. (73) takes the conventional form

HX​Y=−J∑⟨i​j⟩(σixσjx+σiyσjy),H_{XY}=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\left(\sigma_{i}^{x}\sigma_{j}^{x}+\sigma_{i}^{y}\sigma_{j}^{y}\right), (74)

with

J=−827​(J(2)−J(1)).J=-\frac{8}{27}\left(J^{(2)}-J^{(1)}\right).

The global U(1) symmetry is therefore the rotation symmetry in the σx\sigma^{x}–σy\sigma^{y} plane, generated by σz\sigma^{z}. This is an emergent pseudospin symmetry acting within the local singlet doublet, not a physical spin-rotation symmetry of the original spin-11 moments. For spin-12\tfrac{1}{2}, the XY model is equivalent to hard-core bosons through the Matsubara–Matsuda mapping, with the ordered XY phase corresponding to phase coherence of the bosons [17]. In spatial dimensions greater than one, the ground state of the quantum XY model exhibits long-range order in the standard unfrustrated setting [18]. At finite temperature, dimensionality is crucial: in two spatial dimensions one obtains a Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless phase with quasi-long-range order [19, 20, 21, 22], whereas in three dimensions true long-range order persists up to a finite-temperature transition in the 3D XY universality class [23, 24].

Because the diamond lattice is bipartite, the two signs of the XY coupling are equivalent. A π\pi rotation of the pseudospins on one diamond sublattice about the τy\tau^{y} axis sends

τx→−τx,τz→−τz,τy→τy.\tau^{x}\rightarrow-\tau^{x},\qquad\tau^{z}\rightarrow-\tau^{z},\qquad\tau^{y}\rightarrow\tau^{y}.

This changes the sign of ταx​τβx+ταz​τβz\tau^{x}_{\alpha}\tau^{x}_{\beta}+\tau^{z}_{\alpha}\tau^{z}_{\beta} on every nearest-neighbour diamond bond. Thus, ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic XY couplings are related by a sublattice rotation, and the sign of J(2)−J(1)J^{(2)}-J^{(1)} does not frustrate the leading pyrochlore pseudospin dynamics.

The effective Hamiltonian in Eq. (73) should therefore be viewed as the leading nontrivial collective dynamics within an exactly characterized singlet manifold of a local SU(2)-invariant pyrochlore spin model. Starting from the frustration-free parent Hamiltonian (1), whose zero-energy states form the loop manifold described in Sec. III, symmetry forbids a nearest-neighbour local pseudospin bias. The first degeneracy-lifting term appears at next-nearest-neighbour order and takes the form of an unfrustrated nearest-neighbour XY model for emergent pseudospins on the diamond lattice of tetrahedron centers. The pseudospins are not introduced phenomenologically: they are the two local singlet states that span the exact low-energy Hilbert space on each tetrahedron. Thus the projection identifies both the low-energy degrees of freedom and the lattice on which they interact.

The effective Hamiltonian in Eq. (73) has the usual tendency of an XY model: it favours phase coherence between the two local singlet states |A⟩|A\rangle and |B⟩|B\rangle on neighbouring tetrahedra. In the pseudospin language, this corresponds to ordering in the τx\tau^{x}–τz\tau^{z} plane. The resulting low-energy mode is the Goldstone mode associated with slow spatial variations of this emergent phase.

This ordered pseudospin state should be distinguished from a Coulombic U(1) spin liquid. Equation (73) identifies the leading coherent dynamics within the exact singlet-loop manifold, but this leading term by itself does not produce a deconfined gauge field. If a Coulombic regime is realized near this parent point, it must come from additional processes acting within the same constrained manifold. Natural candidates are higher-order loop reconnections and ring-exchange terms around closed paths of the diamond lattice, which play the role of Rokhsar–Kivelson dynamics in related constrained dimer models.

This perspective clarifies the relation to earlier approaches. In the quantum-ice construction of Hermele, Fisher, and Balents [6], the emergent gauge structure arises from perturbation theory about an anisotropic spin-ice manifold. In Rokhsar–Kivelson-type and large-NN dimer models on the pyrochlore lattice [7], the constrained dimer Hilbert space is imposed at the outset and the effective dimer dynamics is then constructed within it. By contrast, in the present construction the constrained singlet-loop manifold is the exact zero-energy manifold of a microscopic SU(2)-invariant spin-11 Hamiltonian, and the pseudospin dynamics is obtained by explicitly projecting physical spin interactions into that manifold. In this sense the construction is close in spirit to Klein-point projector Hamiltonians [4, 5], but with an AKLT-inspired realization of the local singlet-loop manifold and an explicit route to the effective diamond-lattice pseudospin theory.

The two-dimensional checkerboard case is more conventional because the nearest-neighbour perturbation already generates a local pseudospin field. The next-nearest-neighbour terms in Eq. (71) therefore usually act only as subleading anisotropic pseudospin interactions on top of this field. Consequently, the singlet sector is generically gapped: the system locally selects either the |A⟩|A\rangle or the |B⟩|B\rangle state before the weaker inter-plaquette pseudospin dynamics can drive a collective instability.

A more interesting regime can be approached only if the ταx​τβx\tau^{x}_{\alpha}\tau^{x}_{\beta} interaction becomes large compared with both the ταz​τβz\tau^{z}_{\alpha}\tau^{z}_{\beta} interaction and the effective field along τz\tau^{z}. In that regime the combination of Eqs. (71) and (67) reduces approximately to a transverse-field Ising model. The Ising coupling is controlled by 3​|J(2)−J(1)|3|J^{(2)}-J^{(1)}|, up to the common prefactor in Eq. (71), while the transverse field receives contributions from the nearest-neighbour perturbation and, in general, from the one-body term generated by next-nearest-neighbour interactions.

If the Ising coupling overcomes this field, the system can spontaneously polarize along the τx\tau^{x} direction. A uniform ⟨τx⟩\langle\tau^{x}\rangle corresponds, in the original spin-11 language, to a columnar valence-bond state: the AKLT loops predominantly run in one lattice direction, spontaneously breaking the rotational symmetry of the checkerboard lattice. A staggered ⟨τx⟩\langle\tau^{x}\rangle instead corresponds to a plaquette valence-bond solid in which the loops predominantly encircle alternating empty plaquettes, thereby breaking translation symmetry. Such regimes require tuning, since the field appears already at the nearest-neighbour level whereas the Ising interaction arises only at next-nearest-neighbour order. Generically one therefore expects the field to dominate, leading to a uniform local selection of either |A⟩|A\rangle or |B⟩|B\rangle on every crossed plaquette.

V Monte Carlo simulation for equal-amplitude loop superposition

The fixed-loop calculation of Sec. III and Appendix B gives exact control over spin correlations in an individual loop state. A generic ground state, however, is a superposition of many loop configurations, and its norm and correlation functions contain off-diagonal overlaps between different loop states. The question is therefore whether the short-ranged correlations found in a fixed loop state survive in a genuine loop superposition.

We address this question for the simplest sign-free case selected by the checkerboard nearest-neighbour perturbation, namely the product state with |A⟩|A\rangle on every crossed plaquette. This calculation is not meant to determine a full phase diagram. Its purpose is to test, in a controlled equal-amplitude superposition, how the loop correlations are modified once off-diagonal overlaps are included.

On the checkerboard lattice, the nearest-neighbour perturbation in Eq. (67) selects the local state |A⟩α|A\rangle_{\alpha} on every crossed plaquette when Js>JdJ_{s}>J_{d}. The corresponding product state is

|Ψ⟩→∏α|A⟩α∝∏α(|—m—⟩+|ee¯¯⟩)α.\lvert\Psi\rangle\rightarrow\prod_{\alpha}\lvert A\rangle_{\alpha}\propto\prod_{\alpha}(\lvert\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle+\lvert\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle)_{\alpha}\,. (75)

Thus the wavefunction is an equal-amplitude superposition of all products of horizontal and vertical local valence-bond configurations on the crossed plaquettes. This is closely analogous in spirit to the Rokhsar–Kivelson equal-amplitude superposition of fully packed dimer coverings [15], but with an important difference: the objects being superposed here are spin-11 AKLT-like valence-bond loop states, not hard-core dimer configurations introduced as an effective Hilbert space.

The sign structure of Eq. (75) is crucial. All horizontal and vertical dimer products enter with the same sign. Consequently, the norm ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle can be written as a positive classical statistical sum over pairs of loop configurations. This positivity is what makes a Metropolis Monte Carlo calculation possible. By contrast, a generic product of local |B⟩|B\rangle states would contain relative minus signs between horizontal and vertical dimerizations, and the corresponding overlap expansion would not have the same sign-free interpretation.

For an observable O^\hat{O}, we use the standard valence-bond Monte Carlo estimator [25]

⟨O^⟩=∑ℒ,ℒ′pℒ,ℒ′​⟨ℒ′|ℒ⟩​⟨ℒ′|O^|ℒ⟩⟨ℒ′|ℒ⟩∑ℒ,ℒ′pℒ,ℒ′​⟨ℒ′|ℒ⟩.\langle\hat{O}\rangle=\frac{\sum_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}p_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathcal{L}\rangle\frac{\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\hat{O}|\mathcal{L}\rangle}{\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathcal{L}\rangle}}{\sum_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}p_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathcal{L}\rangle}\,. (76)

Here ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} denote the ket and bra loop configurations obtained by expanding Eq. (75), and pℒ,ℒ′p_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}} is the product of their wavefunction amplitudes. For the equal-amplitude state in Eq. (75), this amplitude product is the same for all pairs and may be set to pℒ,ℒ′=1p_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}=1. The nontrivial statistical weight then comes entirely from the overlap ⟨ℒ′|ℒ⟩\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathcal{L}\rangle.

We are interested in the two-point spin correlation function ⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle. Since the spin-coherent basis gives a local representation of both ⟨ℒ′|ℒ⟩\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathcal{L}\rangle and ⟨ℒ′|𝐒i⋅𝐒j|ℒ⟩\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}|\mathcal{L}\rangle, and since the overlap is non-negative for the equal-amplitude state, we can sample pairs (ℒ,ℒ′)(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}) by a Metropolis algorithm. For O^=𝐒i⋅𝐒j\hat{O}=\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}, Eq. (76) becomes

⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩=∑ℒ,ℒ′Wℒ,ℒ′​Ci​j​(ℒ,ℒ′)∑ℒ,ℒ′Wℒ,ℒ′,\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle=\frac{\sum_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}W_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}C_{ij}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime})}{\sum_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}W_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}}\,, (77)

where

Wℒ,ℒ′=⟨ℒ′|ℒ⟩W_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}=\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathcal{L}\rangle

is the positive Monte Carlo weight, and

Ci​j​(ℒ,ℒ′)=⟨ℒ′|𝐒i⋅𝐒j|ℒ⟩⟨ℒ′|ℒ⟩C_{ij}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime})=\frac{\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}|\mathcal{L}\rangle}{\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathcal{L}\rangle}

is the corresponding estimator. For a proposed update from an old configuration pair to a new configuration pair, the Metropolis acceptance probability is

Paccept=min⁡[WnewWold,1].P_{\mathrm{accept}}=\min\left[\frac{W_{\mathrm{new}}}{W_{\mathrm{old}}},1\right].

The structure of the sampled configurations differs from the usual classical spin Monte Carlo problem. We do not assign a classical vector to each site. Instead, each physical spin-11 site is touched by two virtual singlets in the ket configuration and two virtual singlets in the bra configuration. Thus four singlet arrows meet at every site in the overlap graph. This is similar in spirit to amplitude-product RVB Monte Carlo sampling [25], but here each layer contains two singlet bonds incident on every physical spin-11 site, rather than one.

The local coherent-state integral imposes a strong constraint. Both the overlap ⟨ℒ′|ℒ⟩\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathcal{L}\rangle and the spin matrix element ⟨ℒ′|𝐒i⋅𝐒j|ℒ⟩\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}|\mathcal{L}\rangle vanish unless, at every site, the number of incoming arrows equals the number of outgoing arrows. We refer to this as the 22-in-22-out rule; examples are shown in Fig. 7. This rule is the local remnant of the ϕ\phi integration in the spin-coherent representation: any imbalance between incoming and outgoing arrows leaves an uncancelled phase factor and hence integrates to zero.

Using the vertex weights of Eq. (82) and the spin-insertion weights of Eq. (85), we can evaluate both the Monte Carlo weight and the spin estimator for any valid pair (ℒ,ℒ′)(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}). A site that satisfies the 22-in-22-out rule contributes either the base weight 2​π/32\pi/3 or twice this value, 4​π/34\pi/3. Let NN be the total number of physical sites, and let N⋆​(ℒ,ℒ′)N_{\star}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}) be the number of sites of the latter type, namely sites where both ket arrows come in and both bra arrows go out, or the reversed arrangement where both ket arrows go out and both bra arrows come in. Such a vertex has two possible local loop resolutions, which accounts for the extra factor of 22 relative to the base vertex weight. Thus

Wℒ,ℒ′=2N⋆​(ℒ,ℒ′)​(2​π3)N.W_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L^{\prime}}}=2^{N_{\star}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime})}\bigg(\frac{2\pi}{3}\bigg)^{N}\,. (78a)
The common factor (2​π/3)N(2\pi/3)^{N} cancels from all Metropolis ratios, but it is displayed here to show the origin of the statistical weight.

For the two spin-insertion sites ii and jj, the local Ωz\Omega^{z} insertion is nonzero only for the doubled vertices just described. At such a site, insertion of Ωz\Omega^{z} replaces the overlap weight 4​π/34\pi/3 by ±2π/3\pm 2\pi/3, giving a local ratio ±1/2\pm 1/2. Hence the reduced two-site insertion is

χi​j​(ℒ,ℒ′)={+2N⋆−2​(2​π3)N2N⋆​(2​π3)N=+14,−2N⋆−2​(2​π3)N2N⋆​(2​π3)N=−14,0.\chi_{ij}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime})=\begin{cases}+\dfrac{2^{N_{\star}-2}\big(\frac{2\pi}{3}\big)^{N}}{2^{N_{\star}}\big(\frac{2\pi}{3}\big)^{N}}=+\dfrac{1}{4},\\[11.99998pt] -\dfrac{2^{N_{\star}-2}\big(\frac{2\pi}{3}\big)^{N}}{2^{N_{\star}}\big(\frac{2\pi}{3}\big)^{N}}=-\dfrac{1}{4},\\[11.99998pt] 0.\end{cases} (78b)

The positive sign occurs when the two spin-insertion sites have the same local ket-arrow orientation: both ket arrows enter at both sites, or both ket arrows leave at both sites. The negative sign occurs when the ket arrows enter at one site and leave at the other. If either site is of a vertex type for which the Ωz\Omega^{z} insertion vanishes, the estimator is zero. With the spin-11 coherent-state prefactor used in the correlation function, the physical estimator entering Eq. (77) is

Ci​j​(ℒ,ℒ′)=4​χi​j​(ℒ,ℒ′)∈{+1,−1,0}.C_{ij}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime})=4\,\chi_{ij}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime})\in\{+1,-1,0\}. (79)

There is also an extra factor of 33 due to ⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩=3​⟨Siz​Sjz⟩.\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle=3\langle{S}_{i}^{z}{S}_{j}^{z}\rangle. However, we scale down this factor of 3 since the form of Eq. (77) makes the Monte Carlo problem simple and transparent: one samples a positive weight Wℒ,ℒ′W_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}, while the measured quantity is a bounded random variable taking the values +1+1, −1-1, or 00.

The factor 2N⋆2^{N_{\star}} in Eq. (78a) also has a simple physical interpretation. Configuration pairs with larger N⋆N_{\star} have more locally double-weight vertices and therefore larger overlap weight. Such configurations tend to decompose into many short transition loops, whereas long “no-turn-back” loops reduce the number of locally doubled vertices. Since the spin estimator is nonzero only when the two spin-insertion sites lie on the same transition loop, one expects the spin correlation function to decay with distance.

V.1 Sampling a valid loop configuration

We begin by constructing an initial valid pair of configurations (|ℒ⟩,⟨ℒ′|)(|\mathcal{L}\rangle,\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}|) on an L×LL\times L checkerboard lattice with periodic boundary conditions. The ket and bra singlets are then superposed to form an overlap graph, as illustrated in Fig. 8. A valid configuration pair must obey two local constraints at every site: there must be exactly two ket singlets and two bra singlets incident on the site, and the resulting four arrows must satisfy the 22-in-22-out rule. Periodic boundary conditions impose the same constraints across the boundaries of the finite lattice.

The transition loops are traced by following the arrows and alternating between ket and bra singlets at every site. Since each step switches between the two layers, a closed transition loop contains the same number of ket and bra singlet segments. Overlaying |ℒ⟩|\mathcal{L}\rangle and ⟨ℒ′|\langle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}| therefore produces a collection of closed loops of different lengths, as seen in Fig. 8.

Some local arrow configurations force the loop to pass from one crossed plaquette to a neighbouring crossed plaquette. We call such vertices no-turn-back sites. At these sites, once the incoming segment of a transition loop is specified, the outgoing segment cannot return to the same crossed plaquette. Other allowed arrow configurations give a choice: the transition loop may either turn back within the same crossed plaquette or pass onward to a neighbouring one. These possibilities are illustrated in Fig. 9.

In many valid initial configurations, no-turn-back sites form continuous horizontal or vertical strings. With periodic boundary conditions such a string becomes a winding no-turn-back loop. Larger lattices may contain more than one horizontal or vertical winding no-turn-back loop. These winding structures are important because the local updates described below do not change their number or orientation. The Monte Carlo simulation should therefore be understood as sampling within a fixed no-turn-back sector.

V.2 Box update proposal

The Monte Carlo update must preserve all local constraints: two ket singlets and two bra singlets must remain incident on every site, and the 22-in-22-out rule must continue to hold. We use a local box update designed to satisfy these conditions [see Fig. 10].

In each Monte Carlo sweep, we choose a rectangular box of size b1×b2b_{1}\times b_{2} at a random location. The proposed update changes the allowed singlet pattern inside this box while leaving the external configuration fixed. In particular, the singlets crossing the boundary of the box and their arrow directions are not changed. This ensures that sites outside the box continue to satisfy the local constraints.

For simplicity, the box shape and size are kept fixed throughout a given simulation. The update is local when b1​b2≪L2b_{1}b_{2}\ll L^{2}. Because it is local, it cannot create, destroy, or change the winding direction of a no-turn-back loop that wraps around the torus. The number and orientation of winding no-turn-back loops are therefore sector labels for the simulation. This is why the first two rows of Fig. 11 show the same type of no-turn-back structure before and after Monte Carlo sampling.

V.3 Monte Carlo runs

The numerical measurement of long-distance correlations is demanding because the signal decays exponentially, whereas the individual estimator remains of order unity. For any sampled configuration pair (ℒ,ℒ′)(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}), the estimator Ci​j​(ℒ,ℒ′)C_{ij}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}) takes only the values +1+1, −1-1, or 00. At large separations, the mean value is therefore obtained from a small imbalance between positive and negative contributions, while the fluctuations of individual measurements remain much larger than the signal. As a result, the tail of the correlation function converges slowly and requires a large number of Monte Carlo measurements.

This limitation is particularly visible for the largest distances on the 16×1616\times 16 lattice. For example, the diagonal correlation shown in Fig. 11(i) has a semi-log slope of approximately 1.421.42 per lattice step. At the largest separation considered, |i−j|=9|i-j|=9, the corresponding average is exponentially small, while the measured estimator still fluctuates on the scale set by the values +1+1, −1-1, and 00. This separation between the size of the signal and the size of the sample-to-sample fluctuations is the reason that billions of Monte Carlo measurements are needed to obtain stable long-distance data. Larger lattices would require still longer runs to reach comparable accuracy. We therefore show results up to 16×1616\times 16. Simulations on 12×1212\times 12 and 14×1414\times 14 lattices show the same qualitative exponential decay; these data are not shown.

Statistical uncertainties were estimated by binning the Monte Carlo time series. The fitted slopes quoted in Fig. 11 were obtained from the range over which the semi-log plots are linear within the statistical resolution.

Figure 11 summarizes the results for the 16×1616\times 16 lattice in three no-turn-back sectors: a sector with one horizontal winding no-turn-back loop, a sector with no winding no-turn-back loop, and a sector with one vertical winding no-turn-back loop. The bottom row shows semi-log plots of the spin-spin correlation function along the horizontal, vertical, and diagonal directions. In all three sectors the correlations decay approximately exponentially. The fitted decay rate, however, depends on the sector. When a winding no-turn-back loop is present along a given direction, the decay in that direction is slower, corresponding to a longer correlation length.

We do not attempt here to classify all no-turn-back sectors, nor do we study sectors containing multiple winding no-turn-back loops. The numerical results should therefore be interpreted as evidence that the equal-amplitude |A⟩|A\rangle product state has short-ranged spin correlations in the sectors studied. A systematic sector-by-sector analysis, including nonlocal updates that change winding sectors, is left for future work.

VI Discussion and Outlook

VI.1 Discussion

This work establishes an exact microscopic parent point for constrained valence-bond physics on corner-sharing lattices, including the three-dimensional pyrochlore lattice. The Hamiltonian is local, SU(2)- and time-reversal-invariant, and frustration-free: it is built from projectors on triangular faces that remove only the maximally polarized spin sector. Its ground-state manifold can therefore be characterized directly from local zero-energy conditions, rather than introduced as an effective dimer or loop Hilbert space.

The construction combines two usually distinct routes to exact quantum magnetism. As in AKLT-type parent Hamiltonians, the ground states have an explicit valence-bond structure [2]. As in Klein-type projector Hamiltonians, the ground-state space is extensively degenerate and organized by local constraints  [4, 5]. The important difference is that the present construction works already for spin one on the checkerboard and pyrochlore lattices, avoiding the larger on-site spins usually required in three-dimensional AKLT constructions on highly coordinated lattices.

A central conceptual advance is that the constrained degenerate manifold is not imposed at an effective level, as in many Rokhsar–Kivelson-type constructions [15, 7], but instead emerges directly from a microscopic spin-1 Hamiltonian whose ground states are spanned, in an overcomplete manner, by fully packed singlet-loop configurations generated through an AKLT-inspired fractionalization-and-recombination procedure. Local kernel constraints on each triangular face enforce the presence of at least one singlet edge, while global lattice consistency and periodic boundary conditions eliminate states that use both virtual spin-12\frac{1}{2} variables of a physical site inside the same tetrahedron or crossed plaquette, leaving loop states as the admissible manifold in the thermodynamic limit.

A second essential aspect of this work is analytical control over correlation diagnostics within this manifold. For a fixed loop covering, the coherent-state and Schwinger-boson representation leads to a strikingly geometric result: two spins exhibit nonzero correlations if and only if they belong to the same loop, with correlations decaying exponentially with separation along that loop. This establishes a clear separation between local entanglement encoded in loop connectivity and any long-distance correlations, which must arise from quantum superpositions of loop coverings. The manuscript carefully addresses the role of off-diagonal overlaps and their associated phase structure, an essential ingredient for assessing when a loop-gas description behaves classically and when genuinely quantum interference effects dominate [8].

A further key devolpment presented here is the explicit construction of emergent low-energy dynamics by projecting symmetry-allowed perturbations into the exactly known ground-state subspace. In two dimensions, this procedure yields an effective XY spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} model on the square lattice with a tunable bias reflecting microscopic anisotropies, while on the pyrochlore lattice tetrahedral symmetry enforces the absence of such a bias, resulting in intrinsic collective dynamics on the diamond lattice of tetrahedra. This distinction is substantive: on the pyrochlore lattice, degeneracy lifting is governed by genuinely collective processes rather than simple single-site polarization effects, closely paralleling the structure of three-dimensional Coulomb phases [6].

Finally, the Monte Carlo analysis highlights a nontrivial and physically meaningful issue: the presence of topological or winding-like sector invariants that obstruct ergodic sampling under local updates. The appearance of “no-turn-back” loop structures that remain invariant under local moves leads to direction-dependent correlation decay and sector-dependent observables. This is not merely an algorithmic complication but reflects the intrinsic structure of the constrained Hilbert space, underscoring the need for sector-aware diagnostics and nonlocal sampling strategies, as encountered more broadly in constrained loop and dimer models [7].

VI.2 Outlook

The construction developed here gives a controlled starting point, but it does not by itself settle which phase is selected once the exact degeneracy is lifted. The most direct next step is to carry the projection of microscopic perturbations further. On the pyrochlore lattice, the absence of a local pseudospin field means that the important terms are expected to involve several tetrahedra. It would therefore be useful to derive explicitly the loop-reconnection and ring-exchange processes generated at higher orders in perturbation theory, together with their amplitudes and signs. Such a calculation would give an effective Hamiltonian written directly in the constrained loop manifold, and would clarify whether the resulting dynamics is closer to a Coulombic U⁡(1)U(1) regime, as in quantum spin ice and diamond-lattice quantum dimer models [6, 26], or to a confined valence-bond-ordered phase [7].

Another open issue concerns correlations in general superpositions of loop states. For a fixed loop covering, the result is simple: spin correlations are determined by loop connectivity and decay exponentially along a loop. In a superposition, however, off-diagonal overlaps and relative signs can matter. It would be valuable to separate these two effects more systematically: the purely geometric probability that two sites lie on the same loop, and the quantum interference weights with which different loop coverings enter the state. The same distinction should also be useful for nonlocal observables, such as string operators or flux-like quantities defined on the tetrahedra, which are natural diagnostics for distinguishing confined and deconfined regimes [6].

The Monte Carlo results in Sec. V also point to a practical issue that deserves further study. Local updates preserve winding structures and therefore sample only a fixed sector of the constrained configuration space. This is useful for diagnosing sector dependence, but it is not sufficient for a complete numerical treatment of the loop manifold. Nonlocal updates, such as worm moves, directed-loop updates, or loop-surgery moves, should make it possible to change winding sectors while preserving the local constraints [27]. Sector-resolved measurements would then help distinguish physical anisotropies from features introduced by restricted sampling. In parallel, the effective pseudospin Hamiltonians derived here provide a more compact route to numerical simulations of the degeneracy-lifting dynamics.

Another important direction is the study of excitations. Since the parent Hamiltonian is a sum of local projectors, the elementary violations of the zero-energy conditions are well defined. Their motion and interaction under projected perturbations should reveal whether defects remain confined to local valence-bond rearrangements or can behave as mobile fractionalized excitations in an appropriate regime. This question is especially interesting on the pyrochlore lattice, where three-dimensional constrained dynamics can support Coulombic correlations and emergent gauge structure in related models. Understanding these defects would also be a first step toward computing spectral quantities, such as dynamical spin structure factors.

A related question concerns open boundaries, especially for the pyrochlore lattice. The analogy with the AKLT chain suggests why this is interesting: cutting a spin-11 AKLT chain leaves behind unpaired virtual spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} degrees of freedom at its ends. In the present construction, a surface can similarly leave dangling virtual spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} variables, but their number and connectivity depend on the surface termination.

For example, consider a [111] surface of the pyrochlore lattice, as suggested by the orientation shown in Fig. 1. If the surface is terminated so that the outermost sites are the apical sites of tetrahedra above a kagome plane, the dangling virtual spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} degrees of freedom reside at these apical sites and form a triangular lattice. From the perspective of the pyrochlore lattice, these tetrahedra are next-nearest neigbours; consequently, the boundary degrees of freedom at their apical sites are not coupled by either the bulk projector terms or the additional Heisenberg interactions considered in this work. Their low-energy physics is therefore determined by residual surface interactions. Depending on these interactions, the surface may realize different effective spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} models, ranging from magnetically ordered states to more strongly fluctuating regimes.

Other terminations can lead to different boundary degrees of freedom. For instance, a termination through kagomé planes may change not only the connectivity but also the location of the residual spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} variables. The surface problem is therefore not universal in the same sense as the bulk parent construction, but it provides a natural setting in which to ask how local projector constraints, residual interactions and details of termination organize effective low-energy degrees of freedom at a boundary.

Finally, the model suggests a possible route for quantum simulation. The microscopic Hamiltonian contains projector interactions rather than only simple two-spin exchanges, so it is unlikely to arise directly as a minimal material Hamiltonian. Nevertheless, constrained dynamics and effective multi-spin terms can be engineered in several quantum simulation platforms, including cold atoms, Rydberg arrays, and superconducting circuits [28]. The present construction may therefore serve as a useful target Hamiltonian for exploring how valence-bond constraints, loop dynamics, and emergent gauge-like descriptions can arise from local quantum degrees of freedom.

Appendix A Loop representation for the overlaps and matrix elements between singlet loop states

In this appendix we develop the loop representation used in the main text and in Appendices B and C. The purpose is to rewrite overlaps between singlet-loop states, and later matrix elements with spin insertions, as sums over classical loop configurations. This representation is useful for two reasons. First, it gives a statistical-mechanical form for the norm of a wavefunction written as a superposition of singlet-loop states. When the amplitudes in this superposition are non-negative, this norm may be interpreted as a partition function. Second, the same representation gives a simple book-keeping scheme for spin–spin correlations and for the dimer matrix elements used in the effective Hamiltonian.

We shall use a complete local basis of valence-bond states on each crossed plaquette or tetrahedron. It is therefore not necessary to treat all three opposite-pair dimerizations as independent basis states. On the checkerboard lattice we choose the two basis states which we call “horizontal” and “vertical” dimerizations; the “diagonal” dimerization is then a linear combination of these two. On the pyrochlore lattice the labels horizontal, vertical, and diagonal have no intrinsic geometric meaning. One may choose any two of the three local dimerizations as a basis on each tetrahedron. The only essential point is that the chosen singlet-loop states span the ground-state manifold.

The starting point is the coherent-state overlap of a singlet-loop state, already used in Sec. III.2. For a loop configuration ℒ\mathcal{L},

Ψℒ​(Ω)≡⟨ℒ|Ω⟩∝∏⟨i,j⟩∈ℒ(ui​vj−vi​uj),\Psi^{\mathcal{L}}(\Omega)\equiv\langle\mathcal{L}|\Omega\rangle\propto\prod_{\langle i,j\rangle\in\mathcal{L}}\!\left(u_{i}v_{j}-v_{i}u_{j}\right)\,, (80)

where

ui=cos(θi2)ei​ϕi/2,vi=sin(θi2)e−iϕi/2,u_{i}=\cos\left(\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}\right)e^{i\phi_{i}/2},\qquad v_{i}=\sin\left(\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}\right)e^{-i\phi_{i}/2},

and the spin coherent state at site ii is parametrized by

𝛀i=(sinθicosϕi,sinθisinϕi,cosθi).\bm{\Omega}_{i}=(\sin\theta_{i}\cos\phi_{i},\sin\theta_{i}\sin\phi_{i},\cos\theta_{i}).

The proportionality sign in Eq. (80) indicates that overall normalization factors, common to all loop resolutions in what follows, have been suppressed.

Consider now a general wavefunction written as a superposition of loop states. Its norm contains interference terms between two loop configurations ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} and ℒ\mathcal{L} of the form

∏⟨i,j⟩∈ℒ′(ui∗​vj∗−vi∗​uj∗)​∏⟨m,n⟩∈ℒ(um​vn−vm​un).\prod_{\langle i,j\rangle\in\mathcal{L^{\prime}}}\!\left(u_{i}^{*}v_{j}^{*}-v_{i}^{*}u_{j}^{*}\right)\prod_{\langle m,n\rangle\in\mathcal{L}}\!\left(u_{m}v_{n}-v_{m}u_{n}\right)\,.

The fully packed nature of the loop states is important. Every site ii is touched by two singlet bonds in ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} and by two singlet bonds in ℒ\mathcal{L}. Let jj and kk be the two neighbours of ii in ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime}, and let mm and nn be the two neighbours of ii in ℒ\mathcal{L}. The two sets {j,k}\{j,k\} and {m,n}\{m,n\} may overlap, depending on the two loop configurations. The full overlap integrand then contains, at site ii, the local factor

and no other factor in the integrand contains uiu_{i} or viv_{i}. Expanding this expression gives 24=162^{4}=16 local terms. The purpose of the arrow representation below is to keep track of which of these terms survive the angular integration and what weights they carry.

We first define an arrow convention for the ket factors. A blue arrow from site pp to site qq represents the factor up​vqu_{p}v_{q}:

Consequently, the factor vp​uqv_{p}u_{q} is represented by the opposite blue arrow, from qq to pp.

For the bra factors, a red arrow from site pp to site qq represents vp∗​uq∗v_{p}^{*}u_{q}^{*}:

It is useful to regard the blue ket arrows as living in a bottom layer and the red bra arrows as living in a top layer. The colours will then mainly serve to remind us which layer an arrow belongs to.

With this convention, the factor associated with a given site depends on both the layer of the arrow and whether the arrow is incoming or outgoing. The four possibilities are summarized in Table 3.

We also need a sign convention. On the checkerboard lattice, after choosing horizontal and vertical dimers as the local basis, the relevant bonds lie on the underlying square lattice, which is bipartite. We associate a factor of (−1)(-1) with a blue bottom-layer arrow directed from sublattice BB to sublattice AA, and with a red top-layer arrow directed from sublattice AA to sublattice BB. An analogous convention can be chosen on the pyrochlore lattice once one omits one of the three local dimerizations from the chosen basis, as illustrated in Fig. 3. Equivalently, using the site-colouring scheme of Ref. [3], we may restrict the singlet basis to singlets between red-blue/yellow-green sites and red-yellow/green-blue sites, and designate red and green sites as sublattice AA and blue and yellow sites as sublattice BB for the purpose of this sign convention.

We now identify which terms in the local expansion survive the coherent-state integration. At every site there are two red arrows and two blue arrows, each of which may be incoming or outgoing. From Table 3, every outgoing arrow contributes a phase e+iϕi/2e^{+i\phi_{i}/2}, whereas every incoming arrow contributes e−iϕi/2e^{-i\phi_{i}/2}. Thus a local term carries the phase

A useful feature of the sign convention above is that the minus signs always occur in pairs for each allowed vertex, independent of whether the site belongs to sublattice AA or BB. The grey segments produced by these resolutions form closed oriented loops. Each such loop alternates between the two layers at every site of the original lattice: it follows a dimer from the ket configuration ℒ\mathcal{L}, changes layer at a site, follows a dimer from the bra configuration ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime}, changes layer again, and so on. These loops should not be confused with the original AKLT-like singlet loops of a single configuration. They are transition loops built from the pair of configurations ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime}. Since ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} need not be the same, these transition loops need not lie in any single geometric plane.

The common weight w=2​π/3w=2\pi/3 is now associated with every legitimate local resolution. Once this convention is adopted, reversing all arrows on any one closed transition loop leaves the weight unchanged. Therefore each closed loop contributes a factor of 22, corresponding to its two possible orientations.

We thus obtain the following statistical-mechanical representation of the overlap integral:

∫∏kd​𝛀k​(Ψℒ′​(Ω))∗​Ψℒ​(Ω)=(2​π3)N​∑λ∈ℜ⁡(ℒ′,ℒ)2Λ⁡(λ).\int\prod_{k}d\bm{\Omega}_{k}\left(\Psi^{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}}(\Omega)\right)^{\ast}\Psi^{\mathcal{L}}(\Omega)\\ =\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)^{N}\sum_{\lambda\in\mathfrak{R}(\mathcal{L}^{\prime},\mathcal{L})}2^{\Lambda(\lambda)}. (84)

Here NN is the number of physical sites. The set ℜ⁡(ℒ′,ℒ)\mathfrak{R}(\mathcal{L}^{\prime},\mathcal{L}) denotes all legitimate undirected resolutions of the doubled transition graph formed from the singlet bonds in ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime}. For a given resolution λ\lambda, Λ⁡(λ)\Lambda(\lambda) is the number of closed transition loops. The factor 2Λ⁡(λ)2^{\Lambda(\lambda)} counts the two allowed orientations of each closed loop. In what follows, the common factor (2​π/3)N\left(2\pi/3\right)^{N} will often be suppressed, since it is the same for all legitimate resolutions and only multiplies the partition function by an overall constant.

Appendix B Spin–spin correlations in the loop representation

In Appendix A we developed a loop representation for overlaps between singlet-loop states. The purpose of the present appendix is to extend that representation to spin–spin correlation functions. This is useful for two related reasons. First, it gives a graphical rule for inserting spin operators into the loop ensemble. Second, it makes transparent why spin correlations are controlled by loop connectivity: if the two spin insertions are not connected by an appropriate loop in the doubled representation, their contributions cancel after summing over loop orientations.

We begin from Eq. (81). The integrations over all 𝛀k\bm{\Omega}_{k} with k≠i,jk\neq i,j are the same as in the overlap calculation of Appendix A. Thus all sites away from the spin insertions carry the same vertex weights as before. The only new ingredients are the local integrals at the insertion sites ii and jj. Taking the spin component to be SzS^{z}, and using Ωiz=cos⁡θi\Omega_{i}^{z}=\cos\theta_{i}, the relevant local integrals are

∫d​Ωi​Ωiz​cos2⁡θi2​sin2⁡θi2=2π∫0πdθisinθicosθicos2θi2sin2θi2=0,\int d\Omega_{i}\,\Omega_{i}^{z}\,\cos^{2}{\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}}\sin^{2}{\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}}\\ =2\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}d\theta_{i}\sin\theta_{i}\cos\theta_{i}\cos^{2}{\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}}\sin^{2}{\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}}=0\,, (85a)
∫d​Ωi​Ωiz​cos4⁡θi2=2π∫0πdθisinθicosθicos4θi2=2​π3,\int d\Omega_{i}\,\Omega_{i}^{z}\,\cos^{4}{\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}}\\ =2\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}d\theta_{i}\sin\theta_{i}\cos\theta_{i}\cos^{4}{\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}}=\frac{2\pi}{3}\,, (85b)
∫d​Ωi​Ωiz​sin4⁡θi2=2π∫0πdθisinθicosθisin4θi2=−2​π3.\int d\Omega_{i}\,\Omega_{i}^{z}\,\sin^{4}{\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}}\\ =2\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}d\theta_{i}\sin\theta_{i}\cos\theta_{i}\sin^{4}{\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}}=-\frac{2\pi}{3}\,. (85c)

The same formulas hold for the integration over 𝛀j\bm{\Omega}_{j}. The vanishing of Eq. (85a) has a simple meaning: a spin insertion gives zero whenever the local vertex contains equal powers of |ui|2|u_{i}|^{2} and |vi|2|v_{i}|^{2}. In contrast, Eqs. (85b) and (85c) distinguish whether the local configuration is weighted by |ui|4|u_{i}|^{4} or by |vi|4|v_{i}|^{4}, and the two possibilities come with opposite signs. This sign is the graphical remnant of the factor Ωiz=cos⁡θi\Omega_{i}^{z}=\cos\theta_{i}.

These local rules immediately imply a connectivity criterion. If the two sites ii and jj are not connected by either of the two loops passing through site ii in the doubled loop representation, their spin correlations vanish. To see this, recall first that reversing the orientation of any closed loop does not change the weight of a configuration in the partition function. In the numerator of the spin–spin correlation function, however, reversing the orientation of a loop through site ii changes the local factor at that site. From Table 3, reversing a loop through a given site interchanges

|v|2↔|u|2,or equivalentlysin2⁡θ2↔cos2⁡θ2.|v|^{2}\leftrightarrow|u|^{2},\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad\sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}\leftrightarrow\cos^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}.

Reversing both loops passing through the same site therefore either interchanges

|v|4↔|u|4,or equivalentlysin4⁡θ2↔cos4⁡θ2,|v|^{4}\leftrightarrow|u|^{4},\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad\sin^{4}\frac{\theta}{2}\leftrightarrow\cos^{4}\frac{\theta}{2},

or leaves the mixed factor |u|2​|v|2|u|^{2}|v|^{2} unchanged. In the first case the contribution changes sign, since Eq. (85b) is exchanged with Eq. (85c). In the second case the contribution is zero both before and after the reversal, by Eq. (85a). Thus, if no loop carrying the sign change also passes through site jj, each contribution can be paired with another contribution of the same statistical weight and opposite sign. Their sum is zero.

Consequently, the spin–spin correlation function is bounded by the probability that the two sites are connected by at least one loop in the doubled loop representation. This is the statistical-mechanical counterpart of the fixed-loop result in Sec. III.2: spin correlations are not determined only by the Euclidean distance between two sites, but by the probability that the two spin insertions remain connected in the loop ensemble.

The same graphical rules also determine the sign of the correlations whenever the loop representation has non-negative statistical weights. For a single loop connecting sites ii and jj, the sign is set by the parity of the number of steps separating the two sites along that loop. With the sublattice convention used in Appendix A for the pyrochlore lattice, sites on different sublattices are separated by an odd number of loop steps, while sites on the same sublattice are separated by an even number. If the sites are on different sublattices, the non-vanishing local factors at ii and jj are of opposite type, one of Eq. (85b) and the other of Eq. (85c), giving a negative product. If the sites are on the same sublattice, the two non-vanishing local factors are of the same type, giving a positive product. Thus, whenever the plasma analogy is a genuine positive-weight statistical ensemble, the correlations have a staggered, Néel-like sign structure.

There is, however, an important caveat. The preceding sign argument uses the interpretation of the squared wavefunction as a positive statistical weight. If the superposition of loop states contains relative negative signs, then some off-diagonal terms in |Ψ⁡(Ω)|2|\Psi(\Omega)|^{2} also carry negative signs, and the partition-function interpretation is lost. A simple example is the state made solely of diagonal dimers. Its correlations are nonzero along the diagonals and alternate from site to site along each diagonal. In terms of the underlying square-lattice sublattices, however, all sites along a diagonal belong to the same sublattice. There is no contradiction: when the diagonal-dimer state is expressed in the vertical/horizontal dimer basis, it contains relative negative amplitudes, so the positive-weight sign argument no longer applies.

We now give a more explicit graphical representation of the spin insertions. The graphical form of the three local integrals in Eq. (85) is as follows:

Two points should be emphasized. First, the value of the spin-insertion vertex is determined solely by the net flow of arrows between the two layers. Second, the corresponding ordinary overlap vertices have weight w3=w6=4​π/3w_{3}=w_{6}=4\pi/3, whereas the absolute value of the spin-insertion vertex is only 2​π/32\pi/3. Thus a spin-insertion vertex carries one half of the magnitude of the corresponding ordinary overlap vertex, together with a sign fixed by the direction of the net flow.

This observation gives the following rule for the numerator of Eq. (41). All sites other than ii and jj are treated exactly as in the overlap calculation. At the two spin-insertion sites, one may use either of two equivalent prescriptions.

First, one may resolve each diamond-shaped vertex in the same two ways as an ordinary overlap vertex, but assign an additional factor of 1/21/2 to each spin-insertion site. The two insertions therefore contribute an overall factor of 1/41/4. The sign of each contribution is then determined by the net flow of arrows between the two layers, as explained above.

Equivalently, one may choose only one of the two possible ways of connecting the upper-layer dimers to the lower-layer dimers at each spin-insertion site, and omit the explicit factor of 1/21/2 at that site. The final answer is independent of which of the two local resolutions is chosen. This equivalence is the local graphical form of the statement that the two resolutions may either be summed and weighted by 1/21/2, or represented by a single effective spin-insertion resolution.

(−1)s​{2+∑t=1s−12t​(s−1t)+∑t=1ℓ−s−12t​(ℓ−s−1t)}=(−1)s​{∑t=0s−12t​(s−1t)+∑t=0ℓ−s−12t​(ℓ−s−1t)}=(−1)s​(3s−1+3ℓ−s−1).(-1)^{s}\left\{2+\sum_{t=1}^{s-1}2^{t}{{s-1}\choose{t}}+\sum_{t=1}^{\ell-s-1}2^{t}{{\ell-s-1}\choose{t}}\right\}\\ =(-1)^{s}\left\{\sum_{t=0}^{s-1}2^{t}{{s-1}\choose{t}}+\sum_{t=0}^{\ell-s-1}2^{t}{{\ell-s-1}\choose{t}}\right\}\\ =(-1)^{s}\left(3^{s-1}+3^{\ell-s-1}\right)\,.

(ii) One spin-insertion vertex is pass-through and the other is a turn-back. Take, for example, site ii to be pass-through,

2.5,0.5)(5,1.5) 07,1.707)1235270 93,1.707)1270315 07,0.293)190135 93,0.293)15590

and site jj to be a turn-back:

2.5,0.5)(5,1.5) 07,1.707)1250270 93,1.707)1270290 07,0.293)190110 93,0.293)17090 ,1)0.23-8080 ,1)0.23100260

If there are no additional turn-backs, there is a single loop carrying both spin insertions. It has two possible orientations, giving 2​(−1)s2(-1)^{s}. If there are tt additional turn-backs, they must again all lie on the same arc between ii and jj; otherwise the connected contribution cancels. The configuration then has t+1t+1 loops, but for each orientation of the loop containing both spin insertions, the orientation of the other loop through the turn-back site is fixed by the requirement that the spin-insertion vertex carry a net flow between the layers. Thus the number of independent orientation choices is again 2t2^{t}. The total contribution is therefore

(−1)s​{2+∑t=1s−12t​(s−1t)+∑t=1ℓ−s−12t​(ℓ−s−1t)}=(−1)s​(3s−1+3ℓ−s−1).(-1)^{s}\left\{2+\sum_{t=1}^{s-1}2^{t}{{s-1}\choose{t}}+\sum_{t=1}^{\ell-s-1}2^{t}{{\ell-s-1}\choose{t}}\right\}\\ =(-1)^{s}\left(3^{s-1}+3^{\ell-s-1}\right)\,.

The same contribution is obtained when the turn-back is placed at site ii and the pass-through vertex at site jj.

(iii) Both spin-insertion vertices are turn-backs. If there are no additional turn-backs, the two turn-backs at sites ii and jj form two loops. Only the two configurations in which these two loops have opposite orientations give a nonzero spin-insertion contribution, so the result is again 2​(−1)s2(-1)^{s}. Configurations in which the two loops have the same orientation give zero.

With tt additional turn-backs, all additional turn-backs must again lie on the same arc between ii and jj in order to keep the spin insertions connected. The number of placements is

(s−1t)+(ℓ−s−1t).{s-1\choose t}+{\ell-s-1\choose t}.

There are now t+2t+2 loops. However, the loop connecting the two spin insertions and the two loops adjacent to it have only two overall orientation choices that give a nonzero spin-insertion contribution. The remaining t−1t-1 loops, when present, can be oriented independently. Equivalently, the total number of independent orientation choices is 2t2^{t}. Hence the net contribution is again

(−1)s​{2+∑t=1s−12t​(s−1t)+∑t=1ℓ−s−12t​(ℓ−s−1t)}=(−1)s​(3s−1+3ℓ−s−1).(-1)^{s}\left\{2+\sum_{t=1}^{s-1}2^{t}{{s-1}\choose{t}}+\sum_{t=1}^{\ell-s-1}2^{t}{{\ell-s-1}\choose{t}}\right\}\\ =(-1)^{s}\left(3^{s-1}+3^{\ell-s-1}\right)\,.

Thus all possible choices of the local resolutions at the two spin-insertion vertices give the same result. We may therefore either choose one representative resolution at each insertion site, or sum over all four local choices and multiply by the compensating factor 1/41/4. Including the coherent-state prefactor for Siz​SjzS_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}, the normalized correlation function is

⟨Ψ​|Siz⋅Sjz|​Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩=4​(−1)s​3s−1+3ℓ−s−13ℓ​(1+31−ℓ)=43​(−1)s​3−s+3s−ℓ1+31−ℓ.\frac{\langle\Psi\lvert{S}_{i}^{z}\cdot{S}_{j}^{z}\rvert\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}=4\,(-1)^{s}\,\frac{3^{s-1}+3^{\ell-s-1}}{3^{\ell}\left(1+3^{1-\ell}\right)}\\ =\frac{4}{3}\,(-1)^{s}\,\frac{3^{-s}+3^{s-\ell}}{1+3^{1-\ell}}\,. (87)

The factor of 44 in the first line is the coherent-state prefactor appropriate to two spin-11 operators at distinct sites. Finally, by SU(2) symmetry,

⟨Ψ​|𝐒i⋅𝐒j|​Ψ⟩=3​⟨Ψ​|Siz​Sjz|​Ψ⟩.\langle\Psi\lvert\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rvert\Psi\rangle=3\langle\Psi\lvert{S}_{i}^{z}{S}_{j}^{z}\rvert\Psi\rangle.

We therefore recover the fixed-loop result quoted in the main text,

⟨Ψ​|𝐒i⋅𝐒j|​Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩=4​(−1)s​3−s+3s−ℓ1+31−ℓ.\frac{\langle\Psi\lvert\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rvert\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}=4\,(-1)^{s}\,\frac{3^{-s}+3^{s-\ell}}{1+3^{1-\ell}}\,.

We close by applying the loop representation to a state for which the plasma analogy gives a positive statistical ensemble. Consider the product state

|Ψ0⟩=⨂α=1N⊠|Aα⟩,\lvert\Psi_{0}\rangle=\bigotimes_{\alpha=1}^{N_{\boxtimes}}\lvert A_{\alpha}\rangle,

which contains no relative negative signs when written as a superposition of vertical and horizontal dimer configurations. It is an equal-amplitude superposition of all product states consisting of vertical and horizontal dimers on all crossed plaquettes or tetrahedra. Its norm can therefore be represented as a loop partition function,

Z=∫∏kd​𝛀k​|Ψ0​(Ω)|2∝∑all pairings ​η2Λ⁡(η),Z=\int\prod_{k}d\bm{\Omega}_{k}\left|\Psi_{0}(\Omega)\right|^{2}\propto\sum_{\text{all pairings }\eta}2^{\Lambda(\eta)}\,, (88)

where η\eta denotes a global choice of dimer configurations in the top and bottom layers, together with a local resolution connecting the two top-layer dimers to the two bottom-layer dimers at every site. In the state |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle, each crossed plaquette or tetrahedron is in the equal-amplitude superposition of the two basis dimerizations appearing in |A⟩|A\rangle. Hence, at a given site, each of the two adjacent crossed plaquettes or tetrahedra contributes one of two possible dimers. There are therefore 2×2=42\times 2=4 possible incident dimer pairs in the top layer and similarly 44 in the bottom layer. Once a top-layer pair and a bottom-layer pair are fixed, there are two ways to connect them locally. Thus, the local resolution problem has the structure 4×4×24\times 4\times 2, subject to the global compatibility constraints imposed by the neighbouring plaquettes or tetrahedra. For a global pairing configuration η\eta, Λ⁡(η)\Lambda(\eta) denotes the number of closed loops in the resulting doubled-loop configuration. Each such loop can be oriented in two ways, giving the factor 2Λ⁡(η)2^{\Lambda(\eta)}. The common overall factor (2​π/3)N(2\pi/3)^{N} has again been omitted.

Appendix C Dimer matrix elements calculation

In this appendix we describe how the dimer-basis matrix elements used in Sec. IV are estimated from the coherent-state expression in Eq. (54). The same procedure applies to the nearest-neighbour matrix elements in Eqs. (55)–(57), to the off-diagonal nearest-neighbour elements in Eqs. (64) and (65), and to the next-nearest-neighbour matrix elements listed in Tables 1 and 2. We give two representative calculations: the nearest-neighbour off-diagonal element ⟨ee¯¯|𝐒1⋅𝐒2|—m—⟩\langle\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\mathbf{S}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{2}|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle on a single crossed plaquette, and the next-nearest-neighbour element ⟨ee¯¯,ee¯¯​|𝐒3⋅𝐒7|​—m—,ee¯¯⟩\langle\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\mathbf{S}_{3}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{7}|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle on a pair of adjacent crossed plaquettes. All other entries are obtained in the same way, up to lattice symmetries and the signs fixed by the arrow conventions.

We first consider ⟨ee¯¯|𝐒1⋅𝐒2|—m—⟩\langle\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\mathbf{S}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{2}|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle. According to Eq. (54), this requires the matrix element ⟨ψn¯¯|𝐒1⋅𝐒2|ψ—m—⟩\langle\psi^{\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{0.1pt}{\tiny{n}}}}}}}\,}|\mathbf{S}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{2}|\psi^{\,\boldsymbol{{\text{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,}\rangle in the numerator and the norm factors ⟨ψ—m—|ψ—m—⟩​⟨ψn¯¯|ψn¯¯⟩\sqrt{\langle\psi^{\,\boldsymbol{{\text{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,}|\psi^{\,\boldsymbol{{\text{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,}\rangle}\sqrt{\langle\psi^{\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{0.1pt}{\tiny{n}}}}}}}\,}|\psi^{\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{0.1pt}{\tiny{n}}}}}}}\,}\rangle} in the denominator. Here |ψ—m—⟩|\psi^{\,\boldsymbol{{\text{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,}\rangle denotes the spin-coherent representation of the loop state whose singlet covering on the crossed plaquette under consideration is |—m—⟩|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle; the notation |ψn¯¯⟩|\psi^{\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{0.1pt}{\tiny{n}}}}}}}\,}\rangle is defined analogously.

The relevant singlet coverings are shown in Fig. 12. Panel (a) represents the numerator, with ket singlets in red and bra singlets in blue. Panels (b) and (c) represent the two norm factors in the denominator. As in Appendices A and B, the local coherent-state integrals can be evaluated by resolving each vertex into allowed 2​-in2\text{-in}-2​-out2\text{-out} arrow configurations. In the present local estimate we retain only the resolutions that connect the two sites through the local segment shown in the figure. Contributions in which sites 11 and 22 are connected only through a longer indirect loop segment are discarded; the purple turn-back curves in Fig. 12 indicate these omitted connections.

For the numerator in Fig. 12(a) to be nonzero, the two ket strands at site 11 must both have the same arrow orientation, either both incoming or both outgoing. The two bra strands at that site then have the opposite orientation. This fixes the allowed arrow structure at site 22: the two ket strands at site 22 must have the opposite orientation to those at site 11, and the bra strands again have the opposite orientation to the ket strands.

There are two global choices for this pattern, corresponding to the two possible common orientations of the ket arrows at site 11. For each such choice, there are two local bra pathways at site 11 and two local bra pathways at site 22. However, the sites 11 and 22 carry spin insertions, so these local resolutions are not counted with the same weight as ordinary overlap vertices. As explained in Appendix B, one may either keep an explicit factor of 1/21/2 for each such local pathway, or equivalently count only one effective resolution at each spin-insertion site. Thus the number of numerator contributions from sites 11 and 22 is

2×(12×2)×(12×2)=2.2\times\left(\frac{1}{2}\times 2\right)\times\left(\frac{1}{2}\times 2\right)=2.

This is the point at which the spin-insertion sites differ from ordinary norm vertices: the factors of 22 from the two possible local pathways at each insertion site are compensated by the corresponding factors of 1/21/2.

The remaining prefactors have a separate origin. The factor of 44 comes from the coherent-state representation of 𝐒1⋅𝐒2\mathbf{S}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{2} in Eq. (54). The factor of 33 comes from rotational invariance:

⟨𝐒1⋅𝐒2⟩=3​⟨S1z​S2z⟩,\langle\mathbf{S}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{2}\rangle=3\langle S^{z}_{1}S^{z}_{2}\rangle,

so it is enough to count the zz-component contribution and multiply by three. Finally, the sign is fixed by the spin-insertion weights in Eq. (85c). In the present matrix element, one of the two insertion sites carries the opposite sign, giving an overall factor of −1-1. Therefore the numerator contributes

4×3×2×(−1).4\times 3\times 2\times(-1).

The common factors of 2​π/32\pi/3 produced by the local coherent-state integrals at each site cancel pairwise between numerator and denominator.

We now turn to the denominator. The norm terms in Figs. 12(b) and 12(c) contain no spin operators. Hence there is no requirement that the two ket strands, or the two bra strands, at a given site have the same orientation. Following the enumeration procedure leading to Eq. (86) in Appendix B, the number of allowed 2​-in2\text{-in}-2​-out2\text{-out} arrow resolutions at sites 11 and 22, after excluding the longer indirect loop connections, is 3636 for each of the two norm diagrams. For the norm diagram in Fig. 12(b), at site 11, we can admit resolutions of either one turn back or no turn back at all. The same applies for site 22 as well. This produces a factor of 2+(2×22)=62+(2\times 2^{2})=6 for each of the sites and hence we get 3636 for ⟨ψ—m—|ψ—m—⟩\langle\psi^{\,\boldsymbol{{\text{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,}|\psi^{\,\boldsymbol{{\text{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,}\rangle. Whereas the norm diagram in panel (c) of the same figure allows for zero turn back at either of the sites, or two ways of turning back once (either at site 11 or site 22, while the other site is a pass through or there is no turn back), or two turn backs at both sites. So, the total number of different resolutions is 2+(2×22)+23=182+(2\times 2^{2})+2^{3}=18. Along with an extra multiplicative factor of 22 resulting from the two orientations of loops connecting sites 33 and 44, we get the same factor of 3636.

Resolutions at all other sites are common to numerator and denominator and cancel in the normalized matrix element. The only uncancelled local factors are those associated with the two spin insertions at sites 11 and 22. Therefore,

⟨ee¯¯|𝐒1⋅𝐒2|—m—⟩=4×3×2×(−1)36×36=−23.\langle\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\mathbf{S}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{2}|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle=\frac{4\times 3\times 2\times(-1)}{\sqrt{36}\times\sqrt{36}}=-\frac{2}{3}\,. (89)

The same logic applies to next-nearest-neighbour matrix elements on adjacent crossed plaquettes. We illustrate it using ⟨ee¯¯,ee¯¯​|𝐒3⋅𝐒7|​—m—,ee¯¯⟩\langle\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\mathbf{S}_{3}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{7}|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle, shown in Fig. 13. Here |—m—,ee¯¯⟩|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle denotes a state with |—m—⟩|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle on the lower crossed plaquette and |ee¯¯⟩|\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle on the upper crossed plaquette; the bra state is defined similarly.

For the numerator in Fig. 13(a) to be nonzero, the same spin-insertion constraints as above must hold at the two sites carrying the operators, now sites 33 and 77. In addition, the local loop resolution at the intermediate site 44 must connect the path from site 33 to site 77. That is, a path entering site 44 from site 33 is not allowed to turn back to site 33; it must continue through site 44 toward site 77. Otherwise, no single loop will contain both the sites 33 and 77. Thus, this no-break condition is the local statement that the spin insertions at sites 33 and 77 are connected by the retained segment of the loop. With this condition imposed, the numerator has the same effective spin-insertion count as in the single-plaquette calculation. Thus it contributes

4×3×2.4\times 3\times 2.

There is no minus sign in this case, because the allowed connected resolutions have the same spin-insertion sign at sites 33 and 77: whenever the two ket strands are incoming at site 33, they are also incoming at site 77, and similarly for the outgoing configuration.

The no-break condition at site 44 is not imposed in the denominator norms, since no spin operators are inserted there and the norm only requires allowed local loop resolutions. The number of allowed local resolutions at sites 33, 44, and 77, with the same exclusion of longer indirect loop connections used in the numerator, is 108108 for each of the two denominator diagrams. Equivalently, this is the corresponding norm-counting factor for the three sites involved in the local two-plaquette process. To explain this factor in more detail, consider the norm diagram in Fig. 13(b). We have 2+(2×22)+23=182+(2\times 2^{2})+2^{3}=18 loop resolutions, corresponding to no turn-backs at either site 44 or site 77, one turn-back at one of these two sites, or two turn-backs at both sites. For site 33, the enumeration is the same as in the norm diagram of Fig. 12(b), giving a factor of 66. Together, this gives 18×6=10818\times 6=108. All other site factors again cancel between numerator and denominator. A similar procedure for the norm diagram of Fig. 90(c) gives the same value 108108. Hence,

⟨ee¯¯,ee¯¯​|𝐒3⋅𝐒7|​—m—,ee¯¯⟩=4×3×2108×108=29.\langle\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\mathbf{S}_{3}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{7}|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,,\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle=\frac{4\times 3\times 2}{\sqrt{108}\times\sqrt{108}}=\frac{2}{9}\,. (90)

Appendix D Basis conversion for next-nearest-neighbour spin interactions

In this appendix we spell out the conversion from the local dimer basis used in Table 1 to the orthonormal pseudospin basis used in the effective Hamiltonians of Sec. IV.2. The purpose is to make explicit how the leading next-nearest-neighbour matrix elements between physical spin-11 moments become matrices acting on the two local singlet doublets associated with a neighbouring pair of crossed plaquettes or tetrahedra.

The dimer-basis matrix elements in Table 1 are written in terms of the local valence-bond states |ee¯¯⟩|\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle and |—m—⟩|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle. These two states are normalized but not orthogonal:

⟨ee¯¯|ee¯¯⟩=⟨—m—|—m—⟩=1,⟨ee¯¯|—m—⟩=12.\langle\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle=\langle\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle=1,\qquad\langle\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle=\frac{1}{2}.

The orthonormal local basis is

|A⟩=33(|ee¯¯⟩+|—m—⟩),\lvert A\rangle=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\left(\lvert\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle+\lvert\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle\right)\,, (91a)
|B⟩=(|ee¯¯⟩−|—m—⟩).\lvert B\rangle=\left(\lvert\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle-\lvert\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle\right)\,. (91b)

The inverse relations, which are the ones used in the conversion below, are

|ee¯¯⟩=3​|A⟩+|B⟩2,|—m—⟩=3​|A⟩−|B⟩2.|\,\boldsymbol{\overline{\underline{\text{\phantom{\raisebox{2.0pt}{\tiny{ee}}}}}}}\,\rangle=\frac{\sqrt{3}|A\rangle+|B\rangle}{2},\qquad|\,\boldsymbol{{\textnormal{|\phantom{\tiny{m}}|}}}\,\rangle=\frac{\sqrt{3}|A\rangle-|B\rangle}{2}.

For a neighbouring pair of crossed plaquettes or tetrahedra, labelled 11 and 22, we use the ordered orthonormal basis

ℬA​B={|A⟩1​|A⟩2,|A⟩1​|B⟩2,|B⟩1​|A⟩2,|B⟩1​|B⟩2}.\mathcal{B}_{AB}=\left\{|A\rangle_{1}|A\rangle_{2},\,|A\rangle_{1}|B\rangle_{2},\,|B\rangle_{1}|A\rangle_{2},\,|B\rangle_{1}|B\rangle_{2}\right\}.

The subscripts 11 and 22 on the states |A⟩\lvert A\rangle and |B⟩\lvert B\rangle refer to the lower and upper crossed plaquettes, or equivalently to the lower and upper tetrahedra, in Figs. 4 and 5. The matrices in Eqs. (93)–(109) are then combined with the coupling definitions in Eqs. (68) and (72). Summing the appropriate symmetry-related matrices gives the projected next-nearest-neighbour effective Hamiltonians in Eqs. (71) and (73).

A useful check is that the irrational coefficients proportional to 3\sqrt{3} cancel once the spin-pair matrices are summed within the symmetry-allowed coupling sectors. Thus, the final effective Hamiltonians in the main text contain only rational coefficients. This cancellation, which renders only the diagonal and anti-diagonal entries non-zero, is a nontrivial consequence of combining the local orthonormalization of the nonorthogonal dimer basis with the spatial symmetries of the checkerboard and pyrochlore lattices.
